# INC-5521: Oversold stock and stuck holds during the September flash sale

Reported by the checkout team after the 2026-09-12 flash sale.

## What we saw

- The `sneaker-limited` drop had 250 units. We confirmed 263 orders, and 13
  customers had to be refunded.
- The stock dashboard showed `reserved` going negative for two SKUs after the
  sale, and it has not recovered.
- Some customers who retried checkout after a timeout had units held twice for
  one order; the second hold only disappeared when the reservation expired.
- One order was rejected because a bundle item was out of stock, but the other
  item in the bundle stayed held until we restarted the worker pool.
- Finance reports `sold` counts that are higher than the number of orders we
  shipped for a few SKUs.

## Context

Every checkout worker calls `InventoryService` concurrently. During the sale
we ran 40 workers. The nightly `expire()` job ran once during the sale.

The unit tests all pass, and none of this reproduces when we click through
checkout by hand.

A service-wide lock (INC-5490) stopped the overselling in staging but cut
checkout throughput by 90% and was rolled back the same day.

# inventory-service

Stock reservations for checkout. Each SKU has `stock`, `reserved` and `sold`
counters; an order is reserved, then either committed (held units become sold)
or released (held units return to stock). `expire()` releases reservations
older than the TTL.

```js
const { InventoryService, InsufficientStockError } = require('./src');

const inventory = new InventoryService(); // or { store, reservationTtlMs, now }
await inventory.addStock('sneaker-limited', 250);

try {
  await inventory.reserve('order-1', [{ sku: 'sneaker-limited', qty: 1 }]);
  await inventory.commit('order-1');
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof InsufficientStockError) {
    // sold out: nothing was held
  }
}

await inventory.snapshot('sneaker-limited');
// { sku: 'sneaker-limited', stock: 249, reserved: 0, sold: 1 }
```

## INC-5521: what went wrong

Every method read a record, awaited, and wrote it back. Nothing stopped
another worker from changing the record in between. Checkout workers call the
service concurrently, and the store yields on every call, so those windows
were open all the time. Clicking through checkout by hand never overlaps two
calls, which is why nothing reproduced manually.

| Symptom in ISSUE.md | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 263 orders confirmed for 250 units | `reserve` checked `stock - reserved` and then wrote `reserved + qty`. Concurrent reserves all read the same counter, passed the check, and overwrote each other's holds. `addStock` had the same lost-update race. | SKU read-check-write runs under that SKU's lock. |
| `reserved` negative and not recovering | `expire()` released every order older than the TTL, committed ones included, so a committed order's units came off `reserved` a second time. `release()` also accepted committed orders, and two overlapping releases of one order both passed the status check. | `release` rejects committed orders with `OrderStateError`, as its doc comment says. `expire` re-reads each order under its lock and only releases stale `reserved` orders. Status checks run under the order lock. |
| A retry after a timeout held units twice | The "order already exists?" check and the order write were separate awaits. A retry that arrived while the first request was still writing found no order and held the stock again. | `reserve` holds the order lock from the existence check to the order write, so a retry waits and then returns the first reservation. |
| A rejected bundle left its other item held until restart | `reserve` wrote each item's hold as it went, then threw on the item that was short, leaving the earlier holds in place with no order record for `release` or `expire` to find. | All items are read and checked before the first write. A short or unknown SKU leaves the store untouched. |
| `sold` higher than orders shipped | Two overlapping commits of one order both saw `reserved` and both added to `sold`. Separately, `expire` flipped committed orders to `released`, so they were counted as sold but dropped out of the shipping list. | The commit status check runs under the order lock. `expire` never touches committed orders. |

`expire()` also listed orders that were already released in its return
value. It now returns only the orders it released in that call.

## Concurrency model

- **Per-key locks** (`src/keyed-lock.js`). Each store key has its own FIFO
  queue. `reserve`, `commit`, `release` and `expire` lock the order key, then
  the order's SKU keys. `addStock` locks its SKU key. Calls that share no SKU
  and no order never wait for each other. There is no service-wide lock (see
  INC-5490).
- **Lock order.** At most one order key is held at a time, and it is always
  taken before any SKU key. SKU keys are taken in sorted order. Because every
  caller follows that order, two bundles that list the same SKUs in different
  orders cannot deadlock.
- **Reads are not locked.** `available` and `snapshot` are single store reads.
  While a multi-SKU reserve is in flight, a reader can see one SKU already
  held and the other not yet.
- **Locks belong to the store**, not to the service instance. They are kept
  in a `WeakMap` keyed by the store object, so several `InventoryService`
  instances over one store (one per worker, say) still exclude each other.
  A key's entry is deleted when its last holder releases, so the table only
  holds keys that are in use at that moment.
- **Hot SKUs serialize.** Every hold on `sneaker-limited` has to see the
  previous one, so calls on one SKU run one after another. Each call holds the
  SKU lock for three store round trips (read the SKUs, write the SKUs, write
  the order). SKU reads and writes within a bundle run in parallel.
- **`expire` walks orders one at a time** and holds one order lock at a
  time, so it never stalls checkout for more than one order.

## Store failures

`get`, `set` and `keys` can reject. A rejected read means nothing was written.
If a write rejects, whether a SKU write or the order write that follows,
the service writes back the SKU values it read under the lock and rethrows
the store's error. The order record is left as it was, so the call can be
retried. If writing the old values back also fails, it throws an
`AggregateError` holding both errors that names the SKUs to check by hand.

## Limits and assumptions

- **One process.** The locks exclude callers inside one Node process, which is
  how the 40 checkout workers share the service. `get`/`set`/`keys` offer no
  compare-and-set or transaction, so services in separate processes over a
  shared Redis would need store-side atomicity (for example a Lua script or
  `WATCH`/`MULTI`). That is out of reach under the constraint of keeping
  `src/store.js` and those three methods.
- **Crashes between writes.** A process that dies after writing SKU holds but
  before writing the order leaves those units held, because the store cannot
  write several keys atomically.
- **Ambiguous writes.** Rollback assumes a rejected `set` did not apply. A
  write that lands and then reports a timeout can leave the order record out
  of step with the counters.
- **Existing bad counters.** The fix stops new drift. It does not repair the
  SKUs that already show negative `reserved` or inflated `sold`. Recompute
  those from the order records: `reserved` is the sum of `qty` over
  `reserved` orders, `sold` the sum over `committed` orders.
- **Retries with different items.** As before, `reserve` with an existing
  orderId returns the existing reservation and ignores the new `items`.
- **Commit after TTL.** `commit` does not check the TTL. A stale reservation
  can still be committed until `expire` releases it; after that, `commit`
  throws `OrderStateError`.
- **No new API.** Methods, arguments, return values and error classes are
  unchanged. The constructor now throws `ValidationError` for a store
  without `get`/`set`/`keys`, a negative or non-numeric `reservationTtlMs`,
  or a non-function `now`. Before, those failed later with a `TypeError`.

## Tests

```sh
npm test
```

| File | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| `tests/inventory.test.js` | Unit tests for each method, including the order state rules. |
| `tests/incident-5521.test.js` | One test group per INC-5521 symptom. Each test fails on the pre-fix code. |
| `tests/concurrency.test.js` | Calls on different SKUs and orders do not wait for each other, services sharing a store exclude each other, and a seeded random workload keeps every counter equal to what the order records imply. |
| `tests/keyed-lock.test.js` | The lock: mutual exclusion, FIFO order, disjoint keys, cleanup, no deadlock. |
| `tests/edge-cases.test.js` | Store failures and rollback, stores that return live references or random latency, input validation, caller input left unchanged. |

`tests/helpers/stores.js` has the test stores. `GatedStore` stalls one chosen
call, which reproduces the timeout-then-retry timing from the incident
deterministically.

value. It now returns only the orders it released in that call.

## Concurrency model

- **Per-key locks** (`src/keyed-lock.js`). Each store key has its own FIFO
  queue. `reserve`, `commit`, `release` and `expire` lock the order key, then
  the order's SKU keys. `addStock` locks its SKU key. Calls that share no SKU
  and no order never wait for each other. There is no service-wide lock (see
  INC-5490).
- **Lock order.** At most one order key is held at a time, and it is always
  taken before any SKU key. SKU keys are taken in sorted order. Because every
  caller follows that order, two bundles that list the same SKUs in different
  orders cannot deadlock.
- **Reads are not locked.** `available` and `snapshot` are single store reads.
  While a multi-SKU reserve is in flight, a reader can see one SKU already
  held and the other not yet.
- **Locks belong to the store**, not to the service instance. They are kept
  in a `WeakMap` keyed by the store object, so several `InventoryService`
  instances over one store (one per worker, say) still exclude each other.
  A key's entry is deleted when its last holder releases, so the table only
  holds keys that are in use at that moment.
- **Hot SKUs serialize.** Every hold on `sneaker-limited` has to see the
  previous one, so calls on one SKU run one after another. Each call holds the
  SKU lock for three store round trips (read the SKUs, write the SKUs, write
  the order). SKU reads and writes within a bundle run in parallel.
- **`expire` walks orders one at a time** and holds one order lock at a
  time, so it never stalls checkout for more than one order.

## Store failures

`get`, `set` and `keys` can reject. A rejected read means nothing was written.
If a write rejects, whether a SKU write or the order write that follows,
the service writes back the SKU values it read under the lock and rethrows
the store's error. The order record is left as it was, so the call can be
retried. If writing the old values back also fails, it throws an
`AggregateError` holding both errors that names the SKUs to check by hand.

## Limits and assumptions

- **One process.** The locks exclude callers inside one Node process, which is
  how the 40 checkout workers share the service. `get`/`set`/`keys` offer no
  compare-and-set or transaction, so services in separate processes over a
  shared Redis would need store-side atomicity (for example a Lua script or
  `WATCH`/`MULTI`). That is out of reach under the constraint of keeping
  `src/store.js` and those three methods.
- **Crashes between writes.** A process that dies after writing SKU holds but
  before writing the order leaves those units held, because the store cannot
  write several keys atomically.
- **Ambiguous writes.** Rollback assumes a rejected `set` did not apply. A
  write that lands and then reports a timeout can leave the order record out
  of step with the counters.
- **Existing bad counters.** The fix stops new drift. It does not repair the
  SKUs that already show negative `reserved` or inflated `sold`. Recompute
  those from the order records: `reserved` is the sum of `qty` over
  `reserved` orders, `sold` the sum over `committed` orders.
- **Retries with different items.** As before, `reserve` with an existing
  orderId returns the existing reservation and ignores the new `items`.
- **Commit after TTL.** `commit` does not check the TTL. A stale reservation
  can still be committed until `expire` releases it; after that, `commit`
  throws `OrderStateError`.
- **No new API.** Methods, arguments, return values and error classes are
  unchanged. The constructor now throws `ValidationError` for a store
  without `get`/`set`/`keys`, a negative or non-numeric `reservationTtlMs`,
  or a non-function `now`. Before, those failed later with a `TypeError`.

# INC-5521: Oversold stock and stuck holds during the September flash sale

Reported by the checkout team after the 2026-09-12 flash sale.

## What we saw

- The `sneaker-limited` drop had 250 units. We confirmed 263 orders, and 13
  customers had to be refunded.
- The stock dashboard showed `reserved` going negative for two SKUs after the
  sale, and it has not recovered.
- Some customers who retried checkout after a timeout had units held twice for
  one order; the second hold only disappeared when the reservation expired.
- One order was rejected because a bundle item was out of stock, but the other
  item in the bundle stayed held until we restarted the worker pool.
- Finance reports `sold` counts that are higher than the number of orders we
  shipped for a few SKUs.

## Context

Every checkout worker calls `InventoryService` concurrently. During the sale
we ran 40 workers. The nightly `expire()` job ran once during the sale.

The unit tests all pass, and none of this reproduces when we click through
checkout by hand.

A service-wide lock (INC-5490) stopped the overselling in staging but cut
checkout throughput by 90% and was rolled back the same day.
# inventory-service

Stock reservations for checkout. Each SKU has `stock`, `reserved` and `sold`
counters; an order is reserved, then either committed (held units become sold)
or released (held units return to stock). `expire()` releases reservations
older than the TTL.

```js
const { InventoryService, InsufficientStockError } = require('./src');

const inventory = new InventoryService(); // or { store, reservationTtlMs, now }
await inventory.addStock('sneaker-limited', 250);

try {
  await inventory.reserve('order-1', [{ sku: 'sneaker-limited', qty: 1 }]);
  await inventory.commit('order-1');
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof InsufficientStockError) {
    // sold out: nothing was held
  }
}

await inventory.snapshot('sneaker-limited');
// { sku: 'sneaker-limited', stock: 249, reserved: 0, sold: 1 }
```

## INC-5521: what went wrong

Every method read a record, awaited, and wrote it back. Nothing stopped
another worker from changing the record in between. Checkout workers call the
service concurrently, and the store yields on every call, so those windows
were open all the time. Clicking through checkout by hand never overlaps two
calls, which is why nothing reproduced manually.

| Symptom in ISSUE.md | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 263 orders confirmed for 250 units | `reserve` checked `stock - reserved` and then wrote `reserved + qty`. Concurrent reserves all read the same counter, passed the check, and overwrote each other's holds. `addStock` had the same lost-update race. | SKU read-check-write runs under that SKU's lock. |
| `reserved` negative and not recovering | `expire()` released every order older than the TTL, committed ones included, so a committed order's units came off `reserved` a second time. `release()` also accepted committed orders, and two overlapping releases of one order both passed the status check. | `release` rejects committed orders with `OrderStateError`, as its doc comment says. `expire` re-reads each order under its lock and only releases stale `reserved` orders. Status checks run under the order lock. |
| A retry after a timeout held units twice | The "order already exists?" check and the order write were separate awaits. A retry that arrived while the first request was still writing found no order and held the stock again. | `reserve` holds the order lock from the existence check to the order write, so a retry waits and then returns the first reservation. |
| A rejected bundle left its other item held until restart | `reserve` wrote each item's hold as it went, then threw on the item that was short, leaving the earlier holds in place with no order record for `release` or `expire` to find. | All items are read and checked before the first write. A short or unknown SKU leaves the store untouched. |
| `sold` higher than orders shipped | Two overlapping commits of one order both saw `reserved` and both added to `sold`. Separately, `expire` flipped committed orders to `released`, so they were counted as sold but dropped out of the shipping list. | The commit status check runs under the order lock. `expire` never touches committed orders. |

`expire()` also listed orders that were already released in its return
value. It now returns only the orders it released in that call.

## Concurrency model

- **Per-key locks** (`src/keyed-lock.js`). Each store key has its own FIFO
  queue. `reserve`, `commit`, `release` and `expire` lock the order key, then
  the order's SKU keys. `addStock` locks its SKU key. Calls that share no SKU
  and no order never wait for each other. There is no service-wide lock (see
  INC-5490).
- **Lock order.** At most one order key is held at a time, and it is always
  taken before any SKU key. SKU keys are taken in sorted order. Because every
  caller follows that order, two bundles that list the same SKUs in different
  orders cannot deadlock.
- **Reads are not locked.** `available` and `snapshot` are single store reads.
  While a multi-SKU reserve is in flight, a reader can see one SKU already
  held and the other not yet.
- **Locks belong to the store**, not to the service instance. They are kept
  in a `WeakMap` keyed by the store object, so several `InventoryService`
  instances over one store (one per worker, say) still exclude each other.
  A key's entry is deleted when its last holder releases, so the table only
  holds keys that are in use at that moment.
- **Hot SKUs serialize.** Every hold on `sneaker-limited` has to see the
  previous one, so calls on one SKU run one after another. Each call holds the
  SKU lock for three store round trips (read the SKUs, write the SKUs, write
  the order). SKU reads and writes within a bundle run in parallel.
- **`expire` walks orders one at a time** and holds one order lock at a
  time, so it never stalls checkout for more than one order.

## Store failures

`get`, `set` and `keys` can reject. A rejected read means nothing was written.
If a write rejects, whether a SKU write or the order write that follows,
the service writes back the SKU values it read under the lock and rethrows
the store's error. The order record is left as it was, so the call can be
retried. If writing the old values back also fails, it throws an
`AggregateError` holding both errors that names the SKUs to check by hand.

## Limits and assumptions

- **One process.** The locks exclude callers inside one Node process, which is
  how the 40 checkout workers share the service. `get`/`set`/`keys` offer no
  compare-and-set or transaction, so services in separate processes over a
  shared Redis would need store-side atomicity (for example a Lua script or
  `WATCH`/`MULTI`). That is out of reach under the constraint of keeping
  `src/store.js` and those three methods.
- **Crashes between writes.** A process that dies after writing SKU holds but
  before writing the order leaves those units held, because the store cannot
  write several keys atomically.
- **Ambiguous writes.** Rollback assumes a rejected `set` did not apply. A
  write that lands and then reports a timeout can leave the order record out
  of step with the counters.
- **Existing bad counters.** The fix stops new drift. It does not repair the
  SKUs that already show negative `reserved` or inflated `sold`. Recompute
  those from the order records: `reserved` is the sum of `qty` over
  `reserved` orders, `sold` the sum over `committed` orders.
- **Retries with different items.** As before, `reserve` with an existing
  orderId returns the existing reservation and ignores the new `items`.
- **Commit after TTL.** `commit` does not check the TTL. A stale reservation
  can still be committed until `expire` releases it; after that, `commit`
  throws `OrderStateError`.
- **No new API.** Methods, arguments, return values and error classes are
  unchanged. The constructor now throws `ValidationError` for a store
  without `get`/`set`/`keys`, a negative or non-numeric `reservationTtlMs`,
  or a non-function `now`. Before, those failed later with a `TypeError`.

I found no oversell, double hold or double sale under concurrent calls when the store's calls settle asynchronously. The fix still has five verified defects, the worst in rollback and in liveness. I ran every probe in a scratch copy under $TMPDIR, deleted it afterwards, and changed nothing in the repo.

## Findings, by severity

**1. Medium: rollback breaks if `store.set` throws synchronously** (`src/inventory.js:226`, `:236`)
Both `keys.map(... this.store.set(...))` calls run outside a promise, so a synchronous throw skips `settleAll`/`allSettled`. Stores that return plain values are in scope, and they throw this way.
- **Orphaned hold:** a bundle [a, b] with a slow `set(sku:a)` and a synchronous throw from `set(sku:b)`. The restore runs while the first write is still in flight, and that write lands afterwards. Probe output: `order record: undefined, sku:a {stock:5, reserved:2}`. This is the incident's bundle symptom again.
- **Unrestored SKUs:** a fully synchronous store where the order write fails and restoring `sku:b` throws. `sku:c` is never restored (`reserved:1`), the caller gets a bare `Error: restore of b failed`, and both the original error and the documented `AggregateError` are lost.
- **Fix:** send each call through an async wrapper, e.g. `keys.map(async (key, i) => this.store.set(key, after[i]))`, and do the same in `#restore` and for `get`.

**2. Medium: a store call that never settles blocks its keys until restart, and the block spreads** (`src/keyed-lock.js:36-38`)
Neither lock acquisition nor store calls have a timeout. In the probe, one `set(sku:hot)` never resolved. After that, `reserve o2 [hot]`, `o3 [acc,hot]`, `o4 [acc]`, `addStock acc` and the retry of o1 all stayed pending. On the base commit, only the hung call stayed pending.
- **Fix:** add an acquire timeout. A waiter that times out marks itself abandoned and releases right away when its turn comes. Also consider a timeout on store calls, but that adds ambiguous writes.

**3. Low-Medium: calls that share nothing can still wait for each other** (`src/keyed-lock.js:33-37`; the README says they "never wait for each other")
A bundle takes its SKU locks one at a time, so it holds the first while queueing for the next. In the probe, `o-acc [acc]` finished at 405ms instead of about 0ms because it queued behind `o-hot [hot]` through `o-bundle [acc,hot]`. In a flash sale, any SKU bundled with the hot SKU gets the hot SKU's queue. Some of this comes with blocking FIFO locks.
- **Fix:** either take all of a call's keys at once, only when all are free (watch for bundle starvation), or correct the README and doc comment.

**4. Low: locks follow the store object passed to the constructor** (`src/inventory.js:58`)
- Two services over separate wrapper objects around one store: both reserves of 1 unit succeed, while `reserved` ends at 1 (a lost update).
- `svc.store = shared` set after construction (the property is public and writable): same oversell.
- **Fix:** look up `locksFor(this.store)` on each call, or make `store` read-only, and state that services must share the same store object.

**5. Low: API/behaviour changes**
- `addStock` drops any extra SKU fields from both the stored record and the return value (`src/inventory.js:68`). Base code keeps `name` and `reorderAt`; the fix returns only `{sku, stock, reserved, sold}`. `holdUnits`/`sellUnits` keep extra fields via `...item`, so this is inconsistent. Fix: `{ ...item, stock: item.stock + qty }`.
- The constructor now throws `ValidationError` for input the base code accepted, e.g. `reservationTtlMs: '900000'` or a store with only get/set. `AggregateError` is also a new error type. The README documents both, but they go against the "unchanged API" constraint.

## Checked and found correct
- **Invariants under fuzzing:** 1,500 random seeds, with 3 services over one store and concurrent reserve (random bundle order), commit, release, expire and addStock. The store used random latency that reorders calls, either cloned values or returned live references, and rejected about 5% of calls. Every counter matched the order records, with no negative values and no hangs. The only mismatches were seeds that hit the documented restore-also-failed `AggregateError`. The same fuzz fails 100 of 100 seeds on 279eaac, so it can catch these bugs.
- **Deadlock:** the order lock is always taken before SKU locks, which are sorted and de-duplicated. No path takes an order lock while holding a SKU lock, and the service never nests `run` calls on the same key.
- **Lock table leaks:** all 301 lock tables were empty after the fuzz plus unknown-SKU, unknown-order and insufficient-stock error paths.
- **Rollback with rejecting writes:** `settleAll` waits for in-flight writes before restoring, and a failed read writes nothing.
- **expire:** it re-reads each order under its lock, skips committed and released orders, and two concurrent expires don't release an order twice. It matches the doc comment; so does `release` now rejecting committed orders.
- **Retries and caller input:** a reserve retried mid-flight waits and returns the first reservation. Values read from the store are never mutated, and the caller's `items` is copied.

Probe output: `order record: undefined, sku:a {stock:5, reserved:2}`. This is the incident's bundle symptom again.
- **Unrestored SKUs:** a fully synchronous store where the order write fails and restoring `sku:b` throws. `sku:c` is never restored (`reserved:1`), the caller gets a bare `Error: restore of b failed`, and both the original error and the documented `AggregateError` are lost.
- **Fix:** send each call through an async wrapper, e.g. `keys.map(async (key, i) => this.store.set(key, after[i]))`, and do the same in `#restore` and for `get`.

**2. Medium: a store call that never settles blocks its keys until restart, and the block spreads** (`src/keyed-lock.js:36-38`)

In the probe, `o-acc [acc]` finished at 405ms instead of about 0ms because it queued behind `o-hot [hot]` through `o-bundle [acc,hot]`. In a flash sale, any SKU bundled with the hot SKU gets the hot SKU's queue. Some of this comes with blocking FIFO locks.

- **Invariants under fuzzing:** 1,500 random seeds, with 3 services over one store and concurrent reserve (random bundle order), commit, release, expire and addStock. The store used random latency that reorders calls, either cloned values or returned live references, and rejected about 5% of calls. Every counter matched the order records, with no negative values and no hangs. The only mismatches were seeds that hit the documented restore-also-failed `AggregateError`. The same fuzz fails 100 of 100 seeds on 279eaac, so it can catch these bugs.
- **Deadlock:** the order lock is always taken before SKU locks, which are sorted and de-duplicated. No path takes an order lock while holding a SKU lock, and the service never nests `run` calls on the same key.
- **Lock table leaks:** all 301 lock tables were empty after the fuzz plus unknown-SKU, unknown-order and insufficient-stock error paths.
- **Rollback with rejecting writes:** `settleAll` waits for in-flight writes before restoring, and a failed read writes nothing.
- **expire:** it re-reads each order under its lock, skips committed and released orders, and two concurrent expires don't release an order twice. It matches the doc comment; so does `release` now rejecting committed orders.
- **Retries and caller input:** a reserve retried mid-flight waits and returns the first reservation. Values read from the store are never mutated, and the caller's `items` is copied.

I've fixed every problem in the incident report in `src/inventory.js`, with the per-key lock in a new file, `src/keyed-lock.js`. `npm test` runs 99 tests and all pass. Every new reproduction test fails on the original code.

**What caused each symptom.** Every method read a record, awaited, and wrote it back, so concurrent workers overwrote each other. By hand the calls never overlap, which is why nothing reproduced.

| Symptom | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| 263 orders for 250 units | Concurrent reserves read the same `reserved` value, all passed the stock check, and overwrote each other's holds. `addStock` lost updates the same way. |
| `reserved` negative | `expire()` released committed orders too, so their units came off `reserved` a second time. `release()` also accepted committed orders, and two overlapping releases of one order both went through. |
| Units held twice on retry | The "order already exists?" check and the order write were separate steps. A retry arriving while the first request was still writing found no order and held the stock again. |
| Bundle item stuck until restart | `reserve` held items one at a time, then threw on the short item. The earlier holds stayed, and no order record existed for `release` or `expire` to find. |
| `sold` above orders shipped | Two overlapping commits of one order both added to `sold`. And `expire` flipped committed orders to `released`, so they counted as sold but dropped off the shipping list. |

**The fix.**
- **Per-key locks:** each change locks only the keys it touches, the order first and then its SKUs in sorted order so bundles can't deadlock. Calls on different SKUs and orders run in parallel; there's no service-wide lock.
- **`reserve`:** it checks every item before writing anything, and it holds the order's lock from the existence check through the order write. A rejected bundle holds nothing, and a retry waits and returns the first reservation.
- **`commit` and `release`:** each checks the order's status under its lock, so an overlapping retry has no effect. `release` now rejects committed orders with `OrderStateError`, as its doc comment says.
- **`expire`:** it re-reads each order under its lock and only releases stale reservations. It never touches committed orders.
- **Store failures:** if a store write fails, the service puts the SKU counters back and rethrows the store's error.
- **Unchanged:** `src/store.js`, the error classes, the method signatures and the constructor.

**How I checked it.**
- Test stores stall one chosen call, which recreates the timeout-then-retry timing from the incident every time.
- A seeded random workload checks that every counter matches the order records: one service, four services sharing a store, and a store with random latency.
- I broke the fix 11 different ways, including swapping in a service-wide lock and removing the lock ordering. Each break made at least one test fail.
- An independent review found five issues, and I fixed three: a store that throws synchronously skipped the rollback, `addStock` dropped extra fields on a SKU record, and new constructor validation rejected inputs the original accepted.

**Limits, all written up in the README:**
- **Bundles can queue behind a busy SKU.** A bundle holds the SKUs it has already locked while it waits for the rest. If `laces` sorts before `sneaker-limited`, a laces-only order can wait behind a `[laces, sneaker-limited]` bundle that is queued behind the sneaker traffic. Removing that would let bundles containing the hot SKU starve, so I kept it and corrected the docs.
- **A store call that never returns keeps its SKUs locked.** I didn't add a timeout: the API has no error type for one, and the timeout belongs in the store client.
- **The locks only cover one process.** With only `get`/`set`/`keys` there's no way to coordinate separate processes sharing one Redis.
- **Counters already wrong in production aren't repaired.** You can rebuild them from the order records: `reserved` is the sum over reserved orders, and `sold` the sum over committed ones.

The `dx run-gate` command from the guidelines isn't installed, so I ran `npm test` directly, and the project has no linter configured.
